overview: This section separates three ideas the exam constantly mixes up: scalability (handling greater load by adapting), its two flavours (vertical = bigger instance, horizontal = more instances / elasticity), and high availability (surviving the loss of a data centre by running in at least two Availability Zones). Scalability is linked to but different from high availability. For EC2 the mapping is explicit: vertical = resize the instance (t2.nano up to u-12tb1.metal), horizontal = Auto Scaling Group plus Load Balancer (scale out / scale in), high availability = the same application across multiple AZs via ASG multi-AZ and Load Balancer multi-AZ.

coreConcepts.definition: An application or system can handle greater loads by adapting (scaling up/down or out/in).
Increasing the size of the instance — e.g. moving an application from t2.micro to t2.large.
Increasing the number of instances or systems for your application; implies distributed systems.
An application spread over multiple instances/systems, which is what horizontal scaling requires and produces.
Running your application/system in at least 2 data centers (== Availability Zones) so it can survive a data center loss.
A data center (as used in this section); high availability means spanning at least two of them.
Standby-style HA, e.g. RDS Multi AZ, where a second copy exists for failover rather than serving traffic.
HA achieved by running the workload actively on several instances/AZs, as with horizontal scaling.
The EC2 mechanism to increase/decrease the number of instances (scale out / scale in).
Distributes traffic across instances; multi-AZ placement makes it part of the HA design.
The section's named example of passive high availability for a database.
Database/cache services that can be scaled vertically (increasing instance size).

mustRemember: High availability = running in at least 2 data centers (== Availability Zones); its goal is to survive a data center loss.
Vertical scaling is very common for non-distributed systems such as a database; RDS and ElastiCache can scale vertically.
Horizontal scaling implies distributed systems and is very common for web applications / modern applications.
EC2 vertical scaling range in the source: from t2.nano (0.5 GB RAM, 1 vCPU) to u-12tb1.metal (12.3 TB RAM, 448 vCPUs).
There is usually a hardware limit to how far you can vertically scale.
Horizontal scaling on EC2 = Auto Scaling Group; high availability on EC2 = ASG multi AZ plus Load Balancer multi AZ.
Horizontal scalability equals elasticity; scalability is linked to but different from high availability.
HA can be passive (RDS Multi AZ) or active (horizontal scaling).

keyComparisons.difference: Vertical changes the size of one instance (t2.micro → t2.large); horizontal changes the number of instances and therefore implies a distributed system.
Scalability handles greater load by adapting; high availability survives a data center loss by running in at least 2 AZs — linked but different goals.
Passive keeps a standby (RDS Multi AZ); active runs the workload on multiple instances/ AZs (horizontal scaling).
Up/down = instance resizing (vertical); out/in = adding or removing instances via the Auto Scaling Group (horizontal).
An ASG alone changes instance count for load; spreading that ASG across AZs is what gives high availability.

commonMisunderstandings: Scaling vertically does not require a distributed system — it is the typical choice for non-distributed workloads such as a database.
Horizontal scaling is not just 'more power': it implies a distributed architecture, which is why it suits web/modern applications.
Scalability and high availability are not the same thing; being able to handle more load does not by itself mean you survive an AZ loss.
High availability requires at least two Availability Zones, not merely more instances in the same one.
Vertical scaling is not unlimited — there is usually a hardware ceiling.
Adding an Auto Scaling Group does not by itself deliver HA unless it spans multiple AZs (and the load balancer does too).
mentalModels: Think of vertical scaling as promoting one call-centre operator to a more senior (bigger) one; horizontal scaling as hiring more operators.
Think of HA as having a second building in another city so losing one building doesn't stop the business.
Think of an ASG as a headcount dial and multi-AZ as where those heads sit.
Think of RDS Multi AZ as a spare tire (passive) and horizontal scaling as a convoy of cars (active).
edgeCases: Vertical scaling 'up' also has a 'down' direction (scale up / scale down) — resizing, not adding capacity.
The t2.nano to u-12tb1.metal range is the source's stated span of EC2 instance sizes, not a per-family guarantee.
Passive HA (RDS Multi AZ) is an example, not the only form of passive HA.
Load balancer and ASG must both be multi-AZ for the full EC2 HA pattern as described.

whenToUse.situation: Workload is a non-distributed database needing more capacity
whenToUse.use: Vertical scaling (e.g. resize RDS / ElastiCache instance)

whenToUse.situation: Web/modern application must absorb variable traffic by adding instances
whenToUse.use: Horizontal scaling with an Auto Scaling Group

whenToUse.situation: Application must survive the loss of a data center
whenToUse.use: Run across multiple AZs (ASG multi AZ + Load Balancer multi AZ)

whenToUse.situation: Database needs standby-level resilience without app changes
whenToUse.use: Passive HA such as RDS Multi AZ

whenToUse.situation: Instance is simply undersized for one workload
whenToUse.use: Vertical scaling: increase the instance size (scale up)

patternsToRecognize.signal: 'increase the size of the instance' / t2.micro to t2.large
'survive a data center loss' / 'at least 2 Availability Zones'

patternsToRecognize.indicates: Auto Scaling Group (horizontal scaling on EC2)

examTraps.trap: 'To handle more load, always scale vertically.'
examTraps.correction: Vertical scaling hits a hardware limit and suits non-distributed systems; horizontal scaling is common for web/modern applications.
HA specifically means running in at least two Availability Zones to survive a data center loss.

examTraps.trap: 'Multi-AZ is the same as horizontal scaling.'
examTraps.correction: HA goes hand in hand with horizontal scaling but is a distinct goal; passive HA (RDS Multi AZ) is not horizontal scaling.

examTraps.trap: 'u-12tb1.metal is a database instance size cited by the section.'
examTraps.correction: u-12tb1.metal (12.3 TB RAM, 448 vCPUs) is cited as the top of the EC2 vertical scaling range; RDS/ElastiCache are named as vertically scalable services.

examTraps.trap: 'Scaling out and scaling up are synonyms.'
examTraps.correction: Scale out/in = number of instances (ASG); scale up/down = instance size.

beyondSource: Exam guide lists 'Horizontal scaling and vertical scaling' and 'Determining scaling strategies' under Design Resilient Architectures, and 'horizontal compared with vertical' scaling under cost-optimized compute — expect trade-off wording about cost and elasticity.
Exam guide also emphasises mitigating single points of failure and failover strategies, so questions may combine multi-AZ with load balancing rather than testing definitions alone.
